Egypt: Cairo rolls out the red carpet for 80 global CEOs with the Davos Forum, a month before its IMF loan ends

On November 16 and 17, Egypt is hosting in its New Administrative Capital the first World Economic Forum (WEF) “country strategy meeting” dedicated to it. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and his ministers are presenting their projects to 70 to 80 heads of major companies, as the IMF aid program ends on December 15 [1][3][4][6].
The meeting opened on Monday, November 16, at the Grand Egyptian Museum with a press conference by Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Investment Minister Mohamed Farid Saleh [1][2].
According to the government, more than 70 representatives of major international groups are expected; the hosting agreement, signed in October, had announced nearly 80 [4][11].

Badr Abdelatty presented Egypt as Africa's top country for foreign investment “for the third year in a row” [1]; according to UNCTAD, the country attracted $15.5 billion in 2025, while the government speaks of a fourth year at the top [8].

The minister highlighted solar, wind, green hydrogen and green ammonia, and local manufacturing of renewable equipment; Mohamed Farid Saleh detailed a transformation plan, one pillar of which aims to integrate Egypt into supply chains and export networks [1].
A panel brought together the two ministers, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso and the head of the company Sandbox, Jack Hidary [2].
WEF chief Alois Zwinggi sees Egypt as a future trade and logistics hub, citing the Suez Canal's role in global shipping [5].
The day before, Abdel Fattah al-Sisi reviewed the 2026-2027 plan: 5.4% target growth and 3,700 billion Egyptian pounds of investment [9].

Key takeaway: Egypt wants to prove it can attract private capital just as IMF aid stops. According to the WEF, growth reached 5.3% in the first half of the 2025-2026 fiscal year and should stay above 4% until 2031 [3].

The IMF program ends on December 15; according to Reuters, the Fund wants to complete the eighth and final review by then, a condition for the disbursement [6]. According to the website See News, the mission that came to Cairo left without a final agreement, talks are continuing remotely and about $2.3 billion is at stake [7].

The discussions cover economic stability, the business climate and private-sector-led growth in infrastructure, energy and transport [4]. Above all, investors want to know when the state, which is very present in the economy, will make room [10].

Skepticism remains: the government has not published a precise list of projects, and the IMF has warned that a too-slow withdrawal of the state would hold back private investment. For one analyst, the meeting helps advance negotiations but does not guarantee fresh money will arrive [10].

Egypt controls the Suez Canal, through which a large share of goods between Asia and Europe passes. A financially stronger country means a better-maintained canal and a more stable region. And if you're aiming for an internship or a job in energy, solar, wind and green hydrogen are where Egypt wants to attract foreign investors, including Europeans.

Zambia: state mining holding ZCCM-IH wants to invest $2.7 billion and borrow $700 million to triple copper output

On Monday, November 16, the head of ZCCM-IH, the Zambian state's mining holding company, Kakenenwa Muyangwa, unveiled a $2.7 billion ten-year plan in mining, metals trading and electricity. It will be financed in part by a loan of about $700 million, as Lusaka targets 3 million tonnes of copper a year by 2031 [1][2][3].
Kakenenwa Muyangwa, CEO of ZCCM Investments Holdings, detailed the plan to Reuters on Monday: $2.7 billion invested over the next decade [1].
The financing relies on about $700 million in borrowing, up to $1.7 billion from partners, and the rest in equity and internal resources [1].

According to Semafor, ZCCM-IH wants to raise this $700 million by 2028, and the money has not yet been found [2]. The website Miningmx mentions about $300 million in new shares and says the plan must be put to a shareholder vote [3].
The plan combines mining, metals trading and power generation, because power cuts have already reduced copper output in the past [1].
The national goal is to more than triple annual copper output, to 3 million tonnes by 2031 [1].

Yet output rose only 1.5% from January to September 2026, to about 683,000 tonnes, according to the Mines Minister's report to Parliament [4]; Semafor considers this increase far from the pace needed [2].
The government is also seeking foreign capital: on November 14, the minister was courting British investors to reach the 3-million-tonne target [5].
Key takeaway: Zambia is betting on this metal to get out of its difficulties, and the state wants a bigger say in mining instead of leaving it to foreign groups alone [1][2].

Copper has become a strategic metal: it goes into power cables, electric cars, wind turbines and data centers. Rich countries are therefore competing for access to deposits: the United Kingdom is the latest that Lusaka is approaching [5].

The bet is risky. ZCCM-IH still has to find its lenders, and without reliable electricity, the mines cannot run at full capacity [1][2]. With 683,000 tonnes over nine months, the country remains far from the target of 3 million tonnes a year [4].
For Zambia, the stakes are also financial: more copper exported means more foreign currency and tax revenue for the state, which owns ZCCM-IH [1].

Copper is everywhere in your daily life: in your phone, in charging stations, in the power grids Europe must strengthen for the energy transition. If Africa produces more, Europe's supply depends less on China, and the surge in metal prices, which makes this equipment more expensive, may ease.

Ecuador: army kills the front man of a trafficker accused of plotting Daniel Noboa's assassination from Colombia, opposition demands proof

On Monday, November 16, the Ecuadorian army killed in Montecristi (Manabí) the alleged front man of “Loco Ovidio,” a criminal the government accuses of plotting an attack on President Daniel Noboa from Colombia. Five arrests, more than 200 kilos of cocaine seized; the opposition denounces a plot without evidence, 13 days before local elections [1][2][3].
Defense Minister Gian Carlo Loffredo announced a clash on the property of the alleged front man: one dead, five people arrested, weapons and more than 200 kilos of buried cocaine [2][3][4].

Interior Minister John Reimberg accuses Celso Ovidio Zambrano Casanova, alias “Loco Ovidio,” of planning the attack from Colombia, where he is said to be protected by the ELN (National Liberation Army) guerrilla group [5][6].
Reimberg also claims that Citizen Revolution, the party of former leftist president Rafael Correa, was in contact with Zambrano to target Noboa [6][7].
Correa, living in exile in Belgium, called the minister a “liar” and suggested a setup, even a “self-attack,” linked in his view to the polls for the November 29 elections [8].
No documentary evidence of the plot had been made public as of November 16; the suspect's criminal record alone does not prove his involvement [1].
Quito and Bogotá say they know Zambrano's likely hideout and are cooperating to locate him [5].
Key takeaway: in Ecuador, the fight against drug trafficking has become the heart of politics, and every security case weighs on the vote [1][9].

Daniel Noboa declared “war” on criminal gangs in 2024; one of them, Los Lobos, is classified as “terrorist” by Ecuador, the United States and Argentina [2]. Noboa and the new Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella, both allies of Donald Trump, have pledged to fight drug trafficking together at the border [5].

The same day, Noboa denied that the United States has a military base in the country: the American presence in Taura, he said, involves “temporary cooperation activities” in security and intelligence [10].

The November 29 local elections (mayors, prefects, rural councils) are seen as a referendum on Noboa, even though he is not a candidate [9]. A CB Global Data poll gives him a 47.8% approval rating in November [11].

Ecuador has become a hub for cocaine heading to Europe through its ports. What is at stake there, the state's war on the cartels, therefore echoes all the way to drug seizures and trafficking-related violence in France.

Mozambique: opposition figure Venâncio Mondlane on trial for “terrorism” after post-election riots, faces up to 24 years in prison

On Tuesday, November 17, Mozambique's Supreme Court opens in Maputo the trial of Venâncio Mondlane, a leading opposition figure. He is charged with five offenses, including terrorism, linked to the protests he launched after the October 2024 elections. According to a legal expert quoted by the AP news agency, he faces up to 24 years in prison [1][2][7].
The hearing is scheduled from 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. before the Supreme Court, in case No. 52/2025P [7]. Five judges make up the court, and the prosecution is led by two deputy attorneys general [3].
The charges: public glorification of crime, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit a crime, instigation of terrorism and incitement to terrorism [10].
The prosecution is presenting videos, phone taps and bank records [4]. Mondlane denies everything; he says he only called, on social media, for “electoral truth” [1].
He is being tried directly by the Supreme Court because the Council of State lifted his immunity [1].

The courtroom has only 45 seats: national media not selected are competing for four rotating seats, and only one seat is reserved for foreign correspondents [3][5]. The Court refused any live broadcast [9].
In return, it will be the country's first trial recorded in audio and video, with automatic transcription of the hearings [3].
Initially scheduled for October 6, the trial had been postponed at the defense's request [10]. Police called for calm before it opened [6].

Key takeaway: Mozambique's government is putting on trial the man who mobilized the streets against the official 2024 results. The verdict will show whether the opposition can still exist legally [1][2].

The protests he called, from October 2024 to March 2025, lasted months and turned violent [10][1]. Venâncio Mondlane confirmed he would attend, hoping for a trial “without” political “interference” [8]. Supreme Court President Adelino Muchanga says the institution is ready [11].
Press freedom groups denounce the access restrictions, which limit independent coverage of the hearings [5].

The AP agency places this trial in a series: several African opposition figures are currently on trial [2]. In neighboring Tanzania, Tundu Lissu, acquitted of treason on November 6, was nevertheless sentenced to four years for incitement [12].

In the north, in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique is home to one of Africa's largest liquefied natural gas projects, led by TotalEnergies, which is also meant to supply Europe. An unstable country is one more risk for this project, and therefore for diversifying the gas you use for heating or that Europe buys to replace Russian gas.

From Monday, November 16, until the 26th, an International Monetary Fund team led by Julien Reynaud is reviewing Chad's accounts in N'Djamena: execution of the 2026 budget, public debt, the oil and banking sectors, governance and preparation of the 2027 budget. Finance Minister Tahir Hamid Nguilin received the team on Monday [1][2].
The IMF mission, led by Julien Reynaud, is in Chad from November 16 to 26, 2026 [1][2].

How a “review” works: regularly, the IMF checks that the country is meeting its commitments (deficit, debt, transparency). If so, the experts reach a “staff-level agreement,” then the executive board in Washington approves it and releases the money [3].
What's at stake in this mission: determining whether the delays accumulated since May have been made up, while framing the 2027 budget [1][2].

Chad seems far away, but it is at the heart of the Sahel, a region where France long had soldiers and where instability fuels migration to Europe. Canada: Quebecor offers $31 billion to buy Telus, one of the country's three giants, and its shares plunge 15%

On Monday, November 16, Telus, one of Canada's three telecom giants, disclosed an unsolicited offer from Quebecor, owner of Vidéotron, worth about C$31 billion. Telus gained 13% in Toronto, Quebecor lost 15%. Telus's board considers the offer too low and very risky with regulators [1][2][4].
For each Telus share, Quebecor is offering C$6.35 in cash plus 0.17 Quebecor Class B share, or about $19.45: 60% more than the closing price on Friday, November 13, of $12.14 [1][4].

In US dollars, the offer is worth about $21.7 billion [7]. A first proposal had been made at the end of June, then an improved version on November 9, when Quebecor raised its exchange ratio from 0.16 to 0.17 share [4].
On Monday on the Toronto Stock Exchange, Telus jumped as much as 29% early in the session before ending up about 13%, at $13.70. Quebecor fell about 15%, to $65.25 [1][8].

Telus CEO Victor Dodig believes the offer “falls far short of reflecting Telus's value” and sees approvals as the “biggest obstacle” [2]. Board chair John Manley fears a “long and costly” process for shareholders [7].
Pierre Karl Péladeau, head of Quebecor, considers the offer fair and says he wants to respond to new competition from Starlink, Elon Musk's satellite network, and other players [2][6].

Telus has set up a committee of independent directors to study the offer and other options [2]. The deal would have to go before the Competition Bureau, then the CRTC and the Industry Department for mobile spectrum [5][9].
The Péladeau family controls Quebecor through multiple-voting shares, a system that would be kept after the takeover [1][3].
Key takeaway: this offer could reshape Canadian telecoms, after the $26 billion Rogers-Shaw merger [1][11].

Canada has a highly concentrated telecom market, dominated by Rogers, Bell and Telus. Quebecor established itself as the fourth national player by buying Freedom Mobile in 2023, a condition set for approving the Rogers-Shaw merger [10][13]. Swallowing Telus would move it into the big leagues, but would again reduce the number of competitors, which regulators are watching [5][9].

Quebecor's fall shows investors' doubts. Since the offer is paid partly in Quebecor shares, its value falls when Quebecor's share price falls. Quebecor acknowledges it: the premium “may differ significantly” from what Telus shareholders will ultimately receive [1].
Telus shares remained well below the offered price at the close, a sign that the market doubts the deal will go through [1][4].

If you go to study or work in Canada, this battle could affect your phone bill. Fewer competitors often means higher prices; that is exactly what Canadian regulators will examine. On the stock market side, the story is a reminder that an offer paid in shares does not have a fixed value.

How it works: a takeover offer paid in shares

To buy a company, the buyer can pay in cash, in shares, or both. Here, each Telus shareholder would receive $6.35 and 0.17 Quebecor share [4]. The number of shares is set in advance (the “exchange ratio”): if Quebecor's share price falls, the offer is worth less. On Monday, Quebecor closed at $65.25 [1]: at that price, 0.17 share is worth about $11.09, and the total offer about $17.44, far from the announced $19.45. The “premium” is the gap between the offered price and the share price before the announcement: it serves to convince shareholders to sell. If the target's share price stays well below the offered price, like Telus's at $13.70 [1], it means the market doubts the deal will go through.
Precedents: the big moves in Canadian telecoms
March 15, 2021
Rogers offers $40.50 per share to buy Shaw, a premium of about 70%, in a C$26 billion deal including debt [11]. The same day, Shaw shares close at $33.85, well below the offered price [12].
The market already doubted the approvals: it took nearly two years and a court case to close the deal [10][13].
January 2023

The Competition Tribunal rejects the challenge by the Competition Bureau, which wanted to block Rogers-Shaw. It rules that a Freedom Mobile taken over by Vidéotron will be able to compete [10]. Quebecor buys Freedom for $2.85 billion [13].
It was this purchase, imposed as a remedy, that made Quebecor the fourth national player it is today [10][13].
November 4, 2024
Bell (BCE) announces the purchase of US company Ziply Fiber for C$5 billion and freezes its dividend increase; its shares fall nearly 10% [14][15].
Like Quebecor on Monday, the buyer in a big deal is often punished on the stock market when investors worry about its debt or dividend [14][15].

Jaguar Land Rover cuts its forecasts again because of China: its Indian parent Tata Motors falls more than 7% in Mumbai

On Monday, November 16, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles shares lost between 7% and 9% on the Mumbai stock exchange, the biggest drop in the Nifty index. Its British subsidiary Jaguar Land Rover now targets a margin of 2% to 3% for the fiscal year, versus 4% forecast, and £25 billion in sales, for lack of customers in China [1][2][4].
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), a Tata subsidiary, now targets an operating margin of 2% to 3% for the fiscal year from April 2026 to March 2027, versus about 4% announced previously [4].
Its expected sales for the year go from £26 billion to £25 billion. JLR also expects to burn about £1.25 billion in cash, instead of generating it [4].

According to the CFO, the cut comes mainly from China, where sales are falling short of the targets set at the start of the year. On top of that come higher prices for copper, aluminum and petrochemical products, and a larger share of the Discovery, which is less profitable than the Range Rover and Defender [5].
From July to September, JLR made £5.9 billion in sales, 20% more than a year earlier, and a profit before tax and exceptional items of £6 million, versus a loss of £485 million last year [6].

JLR booked £530 million in exceptional charges, including £295 million for a voluntary redundancy plan of about 4,000 people [5]. It is counting on £1.7 billion in savings and new models for double-digit earnings growth in 2027-2028 [6].

At group level, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles lost 5,531 crore rupees (about 55 billion rupees) over the quarter, versus a profit a year earlier [2]. In India, its sales hit a record, at more than 200,000 cars, up 40% [7].
The shares lost more than 9% at one point during the session [2][3] and are down 27.4% since January [7].
Key takeaway: the Chinese market, long a gold mine for European luxury brands, is no longer enough to keep JLR running [5].

The 20% jump in sales is misleading: last year, in the same period, a cyberattack had shut down JLR's factories for about five weeks [6][8]. The recovery is therefore mostly a return to normal, and it does not make up for weakness in China [5].

JLR is the United Kingdom's largest carmaker [8]. The 4,000 job cuts and the savings plan show that the company is preparing for difficult years, between US tariffs, a stalled China and expensive raw materials [5][9].
For Tata, the contrast is stark: Indian and electric cars are doing well, but the British subsidiary, which accounts for most of the revenue, is dragging down the accounts [2][7].

If you dream of a Range Rover or a Defender, know that their maker is looking to cut costs and sell more in North America, not to lower its prices. More broadly, the crisis of luxury brands in China also hits European carmakers, some of which are in your ETF or your employee savings plan.

How it works: why a lowered forecast makes a share price fall

A share price mainly reflects the profits investors expect in the future, not past ones. When a company publishes its “guidance,” it gives a numerical target, here a margin and revenue [4]. If it lowers it, analysts recalculate future profits, and the share price falls accordingly, even if the past quarter improved: that is what is happening to Tata, whose subsidiary JLR nevertheless saw its sales climb 20% [6][1]. The “margin” is the share of sales left over as profit: at 2% to 3%, £2 to £3 remain for every £100 of cars sold. “Cash burn” means the company is spending more money than it brings in [4].
Precedents: JLR, forecasts constantly revised
June 2025
JLR cuts its margin target for fiscal 2025-2026 to 5-7%, from 10%, because of US tariffs, after 8.5% the previous year [9].
Trump's tariffs were the first major blow for a carmaker that exports heavily to the United States [9].
November 2025

After a cyberattack that halted production for about five weeks, JLR cuts its margin again to 0-2% and expects £2.2 billion to £2.5 billion in cash burn, instead of breaking even. Tata books a $228.5 million charge and JLR deliveries fall 24.2% [8].
Weak China was already weighing: a year later, it becomes the main cause of the new cut [8][5].
November 2021
Despite a quarterly loss, Tata Motors shares gain 5%, driven by JLR's strong operating performance [10].
The stock market judges Tata first on JLR: either way, it is the British subsidiary that drives the share price [10][1].

Spain is a major voice in European debates on immigration and climate. A coalition with the far right in Madrid would change the balance of votes in Brussels, on issues that affect you too.

news.2026-11-17-pologne-tusk-nawrocki-tr: Poland: Tusk closes the debate on the Constitutional Tribunal and urges President Nawrocki not to block his law on illegal online content

The standoff continues between Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki. Tusk considers the Constitutional Tribunal crisis “settled” and, on November 16, asked the president not to veto a law on removing illegal content from the internet [1][2].
After the European summit in Dublin, Donald Tusk ruled out any new negotiation: “The question of the Constitutional Tribunal is settled,” he said [1].
He had invited Karol Nawrocki and his family to his home in Sopot for a meeting before Christmas; the presidential spokesman sees it as a political gesture rather than a real offer [1].
Karol Nawrocki sets two conditions for a meeting: the withdrawal of police from the Tribunal and access for all legally appointed judges [1].
On November 16, according to Polsat News, Donald Tusk urged the president not to veto the new version of a law allowing illegal content to be quickly removed from the internet [2].
Key takeaway: it all started with the sudden suspension of the president of the Constitutional Tribunal, Bogdan Święczkowski, which prompted Karol Nawrocki to call crisis consultations [3].
Donald Tusk is asking the president to confirm the judges elected by Parliament [4]; without an agreement, every government law risks a presidential veto, which paralyzes reforms [2][4].
Poland is on the front line facing Russia and a key partner of France. This open conflict slows down its decisions, right down to the European rules on the internet you use every day.

news.2026-11-17-bulgarie-cargo-betul-8-d: Bulgaria: a cargo ship capsizes in the Black Sea after a sea drone attack, the 17th vessel targeted off Bulgaria and Romania since July

On Monday, November 16, the Somali-flagged cargo ship Betul 8 capsized in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, about 40 nautical miles southeast of Cape Kaliakra. Its 12 sailors were rescued; they say two sea drones struck the vessel. An investigation is under way [1][2][3].
Bulgarian military helicopters and vessels from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey took part in the rescue; the crew was taken to the Chaika air base [1][2].
According to two crew members quoted by the website Maritime.bg, two unidentified naval drones hit the cargo ship; the cause and responsibility have yet to be established [2][3].
The ship was carrying 3,000 tonnes of wheat from Romania to Egypt, according to DataPortuaria [4].
According to maritime security company Diaplous, the Betul 8 is the 17th vessel attacked off Bulgaria and Romania since mid-July [1].
Key takeaway: the drone war in the Black Sea now hits civilian cargo ships even in the waters of an EU and NATO country [1][3].
The Black Sea is a major route for the region's grain: each attack raises insurance and shipping costs for vessels passing through [1][4].
The wheat that crosses the Black Sea feeds North Africa and the Middle East. If the attacks continue, shipping becomes more expensive and grain prices can climb, all the way to your bread and pasta.
